title: Ὄνος καὶ κυνίδιον siue Κύων καὶ δεσπότης
titleEn: The Donkey and the Little Dog, or The Dog and his Master
part: The Donkey and the Little Dog, or The Dog and his Master (Chambry 275 · Perry 91)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 275 (= Perry 91). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔχων τις κύνα Μελιταῖον καὶ ὄνον διετέλει ἀεὶ τῷ κυνὶ προσπαίζων· καὶ δή, εἴ ποτε ἔξω ἐδείπνει, διεκόμιζέ τι αὐτῷ, καὶ προσιόντι καὶ σαίνοντι παρέβαλλεν.
sentences.tr: Echōn tis kyna Melitaion kai onon dietelei aei tōi kyni prospaizōn· kai dē, ei pote exō edeipnei, diekomize ti autōi, kai prosionti kai sainonti pareballen.
sentences.l: A certain man, having a Maltese dog and a donkey, went on always playing with the dog; and indeed, if ever he dined out, he would bring something back for it, and would throw it to the dog as it came up and fawned.
sentences.i: A man who kept a Maltese dog and a donkey was for ever playing with the dog; and whenever he dined out he would bring something home for it, and toss it to the dog as it came up fawning.
sentences.n: διατελέω takes a supplementary participle which carries the action, while the verb itself says only that it never stopped: προσπαίζων is the playing, διετέλει the going on. The Μελιταῖος was the small lapdog of antiquity, named from the island of Melite and kept purely as a pet — which is the whole distance between him and the working donkey. εἴ ποτε with the imperfect states what happened whenever the occasion arose.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ὄνος φθονήσας προσέδραμε καὶ σκιρτῶν ἐλάκτιζεν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Ho de onos phthonēsas prosedrame kai skirtōn elaktizen auton.
sentences.l: And the donkey, having conceived envy, ran up and, prancing, kicked him.
sentences.n: The aorist participle φθονήσας is ingressive: not 'while envying' but 'having fallen into envy'. αὐτόν is the master. The donkey is copying the dog's frisking welcome, and his version of it lands as a kick — the joke and the disaster are the same gesture.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς ἀγανακτήσας ἐκέλευσε παίοντας αὐτὸν ἀπαγαγεῖν καὶ τῇ φάτνῃ προσδῆσαι.
sentences.tr: Kai hos aganaktēsas ekeleuse paiontas auton apagagein kai tēi phatnēi prosdēsai.
sentences.l: And he, having grown indignant, ordered them, beating him, to lead him away and tie him fast to the manger.
sentences.i: And he, indignant, ordered the servants to beat him, drag him off and tie him up at the manger.
sentences.n: καὶ ὅς is the old demonstrative use of the relative — 'and he' — the standard way of turning the narrative to the other party. The subject of the infinitives is never named; the accusative plural παίοντας is all that shows it is the household slaves who carry the order out.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οὐ πάντες πρὸς πάντα πεφύκασιν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti ou pantes pros panta pephykasin.
sentences.l: The story shows that not all are fitted by nature for all things.
sentences.n: πεφύκασιν is the perfect of φύομαι and has present force: to have grown so, and therefore to be so — a matter of birth, not of effort. πρός with the accusative here is 'with a view to, suited for'.
